Dear Manjula,
I don't know if I'll send this. It's 3 a.m. again. I haven't slept properly in weeks.
Something's wrong at the centre and I can't say it out loud there. We're told to give up comforts, but the leader just bought a new car with the donations. When Rekha asked about the accounts, she was moved to kitchen duty and nobody's allowed to sit with her at meals. I didn't sit with her either. I feel sick about that.
Every time I think of leaving, I think: who would I even be? All my friends are there. Five years. And they've told us people outside will laugh, will say 'we told you so'.
Maybe you would. I'd deserve it.
My chest gets tight when I walk in now. I pretend it's the stairs.
I miss you. I'm sorry I stopped calling.
Devika

qa.q: What did the leader buy with the donations?
qa.a: The leader just bought a new car with the donations.

qa.q: How does Devika feel at the thought of leaving the centre, and what shows it?
qa.a: Devika feels afraid and ashamed: leaving raises 'who would I even be?', means losing five years of friends, and Devika expects to be laughed at and even to deserve it.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Devika right now?
qa.a: Devika could send this letter or call Manjula, and speak to a counsellor, so the doubts have somewhere safe to go.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel if this letter arrives after years of silence?
qa.a: Manjula may feel relieved to hear from Devika and worried by the sleepless nights, and eager to respond without judgement.

Uma, you promised you wouldn't tell anyone. Okay. I'm just going to say it.
Something doesn't add up. At the meetings they say everyone is equal, but when I asked why the same three people always decide everything, I was told to 'work on my ego'. Last month Karthik was told to leave the group chat for missing two sessions because his mother was in hospital. Nobody said anything. I didn't say anything.
Since then I can't sleep. I lie there going over it. My stomach's always in a knot. I feel guilty for even thinking this, like I'm betraying them.
And if I say it, what happens? I lose everyone. Four years of friends. They say people who leave end up alone, and that outsiders only pretend to care.
You don't only pretend, do you?
Sorry. I'm Pankaj, still the same idiot who talks too much. Tell me I'm not crazy.

qa.a: Uma may feel both moved and worried, realising how isolated and afraid Pankaj has become.

Sunday, 3 a.m.
Can't sleep again. Third night this week.
Today at the gathering, Trisha asked why the leaders eat separately and why our contributions went up again. Just asked. She was taken to the side room, and afterwards we were told not to speak to her for a week. She sat alone at lunch with her plate, and I walked past her. I walked past her.
We're taught that doubt is the outside world creeping in. But the leaders promised last year there'd be no more rises. That was a promise. And Trisha is the kindest person there.
If I say anything, I'll be in the side room too. Everyone I love now is inside. Outside, my parents probably think I'm a fool. I don't know which is worse.
My stomach hurts. I feel guilty for even writing this. I'll tear this page out in the morning.
Vinita

qa.a: Why the leaders eat separately and why our contributions went up again.

qa.q: What is Vinita feeling at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: Vinita feels anxious, sleepless and guilty, torn between noticing unfairness and fearing punishment and the loss of everyone inside.

qa.a: Trisha feels isolated and humiliated, punished with silence for asking a question, even by people she thought were friends.

The commune sat above the apple orchards outside Kullu, and at five every morning Himani joined the others in the silent walk. For two years it had felt like peace.
Then Sonali, who had given the commune her savings and her car, asked in the evening meeting why the founder's family lived in the new stone house while everyone else slept in the cold dorm. Next morning Sonali's bed was empty. The founder said she had "chosen the outside" and that nobody should contact her.
Himani began lying awake listening to the river. She kept remembering things: the promise that everyone would share the house by winter; her mother's letters she had been told to leave unopened. Each time a question rose, she heard the founder's voice: doubt is the enemy's door.
She could barely eat. When the others laughed at dinner she laughed too, a beat late, and felt ashamed of how easily she could pretend.

qa.q: Where did the founder's family live?
qa.a: In the new stone house.

qa.q: What does Himani's late laugh at dinner reveal?
qa.a: She feels anxious and ashamed, pretending to belong while doubts about fairness keep her awake.

qa.q: What could open a way out for Himani?
qa.a: Opening her mother's letters or finding Sonali, trusted outside links that could give her doubts somewhere safe to go.

qa.q: What might Sonali be going through after leaving?
qa.a: Sonali is likely frightened and alone, cut off from friends after giving the commune her savings and car.

grounding: In a rural commune a member sees unfair treatment and broken promises, but fear and warnings about outsiders keep her doubts silent.

passage: In the shared house outside Lisbon, the rule was that everyone gave their weekend to the movement's bookshop. Sofia had given two years of weekends. Last Friday the leaders announced that Thabo, who had worked there longest, was "stepping away to reflect" after he asked why the donations never appeared in the accounts. Sofia had wondered the same thing for months. She said nothing at the meeting. Nobody did. That night she lay awake listening to the trams, rehearsing a question and then imagining the room turning to look at her. If she left, who would she even have? The leaders said the world outside was cruel to people like them. At breakfast she smiled, passed the bread, and felt guilty for the thought she had not spoken. By Sunday her jaw ached from clenching it in her sleep.
